title: An Astrobiologist’s Guide to the Best Sci-Fi Reads
gist: Astrobiologist and author Seven Rasmussen reviews seven science-fiction novels through the lens of real science, evaluating each book's speculative biology, physics, or geoscience for scientific plausibility rather than just literary merit.

themes.theme: Somaforming in To Be Taught, If Fortunate

insights.claim: In Becky Chambers' To Be Taught, If Fortunate, explorers use CRISPR-based 'somaforming' technology to adapt their own bodies to alien environments, such as radiation resistance or extra muscle for high gravity, rather than terraforming the planet to suit them.
insights.speaker: Seven Rasmussen
insights.so_what: Rasmussen judges this body-adaptation concept as futuristic but not scientifically impossible, given plausible timescales for cellular regeneration between planetary visits.
insights.quote: Chambers’ explorers wake up from cold sleep on new planets with changed bodies: resistant to extreme radiation, or muscular enough to endure excess gravity. The CRISPR-based physiology-altering tech is futuristic for sure, but not impossible, especially given the long time for cellular regeneration between planets.
insights.locator: To Be Taught If Fortunate by Becky Chambers

themes.theme: Geokinetic energy in The Fifth Season

insights.claim: N.K. Jemisin's The Fifth Season, first in her triple-Hugo-Award-winning trilogy, centers on 'orogenes,' people who manipulate geokinetic energy, on a distant-future Earth dominated by volcanic and seismic activity.
insights.speaker: Seven Rasmussen
insights.so_what: Rasmussen finds Jemisin's use of seismology as both plot device and philosophical theme scientifically compelling even while questioning the plausibility of the underlying fragile geosphere premise.
insights.quote: It tells the intertwined stories of three “orogenes”—people who, for better or for worse, can manipulate geokinetic energy. On a volatile distant-future Earth where the novel is set, the climate is dominated by volcanic and seismic activity.
insights.locator: The Fifth Season by N. K. Jemisin

themes.theme: Orbital astrophysics in Gideon the Ninth

insights.claim: Tamsyn Muir's Gideon the Ninth is set in a resurrected solar system with an undead sun and nine dynastic 'houses' spread across the eight planets and Pluto, with the setting's physical locations, such as orbital space stations and Pluto's deep-core Ninth House, kept close to real astrophysics.
insights.speaker: Seven Rasmussen
insights.so_what: Rasmussen singles out this novel as one where the fantastical premise (necromancy) coexists with a setting geography that holds up to astrophysical scrutiny.
insights.quote: Many of these seats of power are physically located in orbital space stations; Earth’s First House is on the surface, Pluto’s Ninth House plunges deep into the dwarf planet’s core.
insights.locator: Gideon the Ninth by Tamsyn Muir

insights.claim: Dan Simmons' Hyperion features the sub-lightspeed Hawking Drive, which causes a scientifically plausible 'time debt,' and the near-instantaneous Gideon Drive, which kills and then resurrects its passengers.
insights.speaker: Seven Rasmussen
insights.so_what: Rasmussen rates the Hawking Drive's relativistic time-debt effect as scientifically accurate and feasible, distinguishing it from the more fantastical Gideon Drive.
insights.quote: The sub-lightspeed Hawking Drive causes “time debt” (accurate! feasible!). The near-instantaneous Gideon Drive kills and then resurrects its passengers (delightfully morbid! religious trauma undertones! tragically unrealistic).

insights.claim: Rasmussen calls Hyperion, a cyberpunk space-opera retelling of the Canterbury Tales, her favorite book of all time for its seamless blend of hard science fiction and space fantasy.
insights.speaker: Seven Rasmussen
insights.so_what: Signals which of the seven reviewed books the author personally rates most highly, for readers weighing where to start.
insights.quote: The seamless blend of hard sci-fi and space fantasy makes Hyperion my favorite book of all time.

insights.claim: Jeff VanderMeer's Annihilation uses uncanny biological concepts, including cryptic messages written in human brain cells and wildlife that undergoes mitosis before the reader's eyes, that Rasmussen says would likely draw U.N. sanctions if attempted in a real lab.
insights.speaker: Seven Rasmussen
insights.so_what: Frames Annihilation's biology as imaginative rather than plausible science, distinguishing it from the harder-science entries on the list.
insights.quote: Both versions use uncanny biology to great effect, whether it’s cryptic messages written in human brain cells or wildlife that mitoses before our eyes. Recreating either of these concepts in the lab would probably result in U.N. sanctions, so perhaps they’re best left in mad scientist territory.

themes.theme: Many-worlds quantum mechanics in This Is How You Lose the Time War

insights.claim: Amal El-Mohtar and Max Gladstone's This Is How You Lose the Time War adheres closely to the 'many-worlds' interpretation of quantum mechanics, where every outcome of every event splits into its own universe.
insights.speaker: Seven Rasmussen
insights.so_what: Rasmussen recommends this book as required reading for quantum physics students specifically for its rigorous adherence to a real physics interpretation.
insights.quote: As far as time travel stories go, this one is one of my favorites for its airtight adherence to the “many worlds” interpretation of quantum mechanics—the notion that every outcome of every event splits into its own universe. 10/10, should be required reading for students of quantum physics.
insights.locator: This Is How You Lose The Time War

themes.theme: Rapid virus-driven evolution in Children of Time

insights.claim: In Adrian Tchaikovsky's Children of Time, a nanovirus intended to accelerate human evolution on a new planet misses its target and instead accelerates the evolution of a spider species, producing an entire spider civilization with its own architecture, language, and fiction.
insights.speaker: Seven Rasmussen
insights.so_what: Rasmussen praises the novel's world-building and culture-building around the spider civilization even while flagging the premise's core biological mechanism as scientifically weak.
insights.quote: The spider society—including spider architecture, spider language, spider fiction archetypes, and more—is a master class in not just world-building but culture-building that I’m still thinking about over a decade later.
insights.locator: Children of Time by Adrian Tchaikovsky

insights.claim: Rasmussen finds the science in Children of Time 'iffy,' noting it is hard to imagine a single virus adaptable enough to guide an entire species to technological prowess.
insights.speaker: Seven Rasmussen
insights.so_what: Shows the author is willing to critique even beloved books' scientific plausibility rather than giving every pick a pass.
insights.quote: But the science is iffy. I find it hard to imagine a single virus adaptable enough to guide an entire species to technological prowess.
insights.locator: Children of Time by Adrian Tchaikovsky
